figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. Discovery of roseomycins A and B through deletion of the daptomycin BGC. (A) Linking metabolites to biosynthetic gene clusters
(BGCs). The genes are color-coded as follows: red (core biosynthetic genes), orange (additional biosynthetic genes), light blue (transporter
genes), green (transcriptional regulator genes), and gray (unknown genes). Deletion of the daptomycin BGC resulted in the enhanced production
of three distinct metabolite groups. LC-MS analysis linked Group B to the collismycin BGC and Group C to the arylomycin BGC. However, the
metabolite group A remained cryptic. (B) Relative production of three metabolite groups in the dpt-deletion mutant of S. roseosporus NRRL 11379
compared to the wild type. Asterisks represent p-values *<0.05, **<0.01, and ***<0.001, as determined by a two-tailed Student’s t-test. Graphs
represent the mean of three replicates. (C) Structural elucidation and chemical structures of roseomycins A (1a) and B (1b).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Identification and heterologous expression of the roseomycin BGC. (A) The roseomycin BGC and its gene annotation. The putative
roseomycin BGC, designated as the roy cluster, was identified from the genome of Streptomyces roseosporus by searching for genes responsible for
the CDG biosynthesis. (B) Metabolome analysis of Streptomyces albus J1074 harboring the roy cluster. Cloning of the roy cluster and its
heterologous expression in S. albus produced roseomycins A and B together with two additional metabolites. (C) Metabolome analysis of S. albus
harboring the promoter-engineered roy cluster. Two native promoters, one unidirectional promoter (P1) and one bidirectional promoter (P2), in
the roy cluster were replaced with synthetic promoters by CRISPR-mediated yeast recombination. Although no change in the metabolite profile was
observed, this promoter engineering increased the production levels of 2b and 3b. (D) The chemical structures of roseomycins C (2b) and D (3b).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Proposed biosynthesis of roseomycin D (3b) based on a gene deletion study. (A) Proposed biosynthesis of roseomycin D (3b). The
function of each biosynthetic gene was inferred based on the metabolite profiles of the corresponding gene deletion mutants. (B) Metabolite
profiles of deletion mutants lacking ATP-grasp ligase genes, including royP, royM, and royF. Deletion of royF abolished the production of 3b. (C)
Metabolite profiles of deletion mutants of the CDG core biosynthetic gene royI and the amide synthetase gene royL. Deletion of royI halted the
production of all roseomycin-related metabolites, while deletion of royL led to the accumulation of the CDG intermediate. (D) Metabolite profiles
of deletion mutants of two amino acid modification enzyme genes: royG, with homology to TauD dioxygenase, and royH, with homology to fatty
acid desaturase. Deletion of royG abolished the production of 3b, while deletion of royH abolished all b-series metabolites containing a double bond
in L-Lys.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. In vitro characterization of amide-bond forming activity of RoyL. (A) Comparison of the catalytic activities between RoyL and ToyM.
RoyL is an amide-bond-forming enzyme that utilizes CDG and L-Lys as substrates, whereas ToyM is a nitrile-forming enzyme that uses CDG and
ammonia (NH3) as substrates. (B) In vitro characterization of ToyM and RoyL using CDG (4) as the carboxyl acid substrate and various amine
donors, including L-Nα-Ac-Lys, L-Lys, and NH3. ToyM exclusively reacted with NH3, while RoyL showed broad substrate specificity. (C) In vitro
substrate scope analysis of RoyL using a panel of amino acid substrates. RoyL accepted L-Orn, L-Dab, and L-Dap as amine substrates, all of which
contain side-chain amines of varying carbon lengths. Among L-His, L-Gln, L-Asn, and L-Arg, RoyL only used L-Arg as an amine substrate. (D)
Chemical structures of the enzymatic products roseomycins E−H (6−9).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. In silico modeling and site-directed mutagenesis of RoyL to identify key catalytic residues. (A) Putative active site of RoyL and its
substrate binding. In silico modeling suggests that Y41, H45, and E48 are likely to be the key residues for amide bond formation between L-lysine
and adenylated 7-carboxy-7-deazaguanine (AMP-CDG). D132, D138, and C139 are involved in the recognition of AMP-CDG. (B) Metabolite
profile of the CDG operon coexpressed with RoyL variants in S. albus J1074. Compounds 1a and 2a were the major products of the coexpression of
wild-type RoyL. The variants C139A, D138A, R104A, E48A, H45A, and Y41A completely abolished the RoyL activity, indicating a crucial role of
these residues in amide bond formation. (C) Relative in vivo activities of RoyL variants. The bars represent the means of n = 3 independent
experiments, and the error bars indicate the standard deviation, marked as red round symbols. All experiments were repeated independently three
times with similar results.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 6. Phylogeny-based mining of DABS genes from Actinobacteria and their functional characterization. (A) Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic
tree of deazapurine amide bond synthetases (DABSs) from Actinobacteria. Functionally characterized DABSs are marked with red asterisks. In vivo
functional characterization revealed the amine substrate associated with each clade. (B) Representative BGCs containing four DABS subfamilies.
CDG biosynthetic genes, including GTP cyclohydrolase I, 6-carboxytetrahydropterin synthase, 7-carboxy-7-deazaguanine synthase, and 7-cyano-7-
deazaguanine synthase, are shown in yellow. DABS genes are highlighted in red. (C) Metabolite profiles of S. albus coexpressing the CDG operon
and each DABS gene.
